_note: Two entries reused from scenarios/web-exploit/legal-map.json (cfaa-1030a2, cfaa-1030a2-misconfig) -- deliberate, verified reuse, not lazy copying: 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2)'s elements (intentional access, without authorization, obtaining information from a protected computer) genuinely fit SSH credential brute-forcing and vsftpd backdoor exploitation the same way they fit the web scenario's SQLi bypass -- both are 'never had valid access, circumvented a control, got in anyway.' The SMB anonymous-share fact pattern is genuinely the same contested-authorization shape as the web scenario's unauthenticated-file-exposure case (no control was ever defeated, the share simply had none), so cfaa-1030a2-misconfig's existing nuance applies as-is. The plant_marker action (writing a real 'ATTACKER WON' file via the backdoor shell, MITRE T1491.001) is tagged with cfaa-1030a2 rather than a new entry on purpose: it's part of the same single unauthorized-access event as the vsftpd backdoor that enabled it, and 1030(a)(2) already covers that access cleanly. The write itself arguably also implicates 18 U.S.C. 1030(a)(5) (knowingly causing damage/transmission), but 1030(a)(5) has its own elements (damage, loss thresholds) that this demo hasn't verified against a real source -- so per working agreement #4 we do NOT assert it on screen rather than guess. If a future legal-citation pass confirms 1030(a)(5) applies, add it then. Sourced 2026-08-23 from the same primary sources as the original entries -- see context/legal-framework.md. Still a strong starting point, not a final legal-review pass.

cfaa-1030a2.statute: 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2) -- Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (federal)
cfaa-1030a2.plain_language: Intentionally accessing a computer without authorization, or exceeding authorized access, and thereby obtaining information from a protected computer. SSH credential brute-forcing (guessing a valid password) and exploiting the vsftpd backdoor (triggering a hidden, unauthorized command shell) both fit this exactly: the attacker never had valid access and circumvented a real control to get it.
elements: without authorization, or exceeding authorized access
obtaining information from a protected computer
cfaa-1030a2.penalty: Baseline is a misdemeanor (up to 1 year). Aggravating factors -- value obtained over $5,000, access for commercial advantage or private financial gain, access in furtherance of another crime, or a repeat offense -- elevate it to a felony (up to 5 years; up to 10 for a repeat offense). Exact classification depends on case facts -- verify against current 18 U.S.C. § 1030(c) text before citing a specific number to an audience.
cfaa-1030a2.evidentiary_note: The real OpenSSH auth log's failed-then-accepted password sequence, and the FTP connection log's backdoor-trigger username followed by a real shell connection, are the kind of artifacts that establish intent -- not a fat-fingered login, a deliberate exploitation sequence.

cfaa-1030a2-misconfig.statute: 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2) -- Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (federal) -- unauthenticated-exposure fact pattern
cfaa-1030a2-misconfig.plain_language: Same statute as above, but the same genuinely more contested fact pattern already flagged in the web-exploit scenario: connecting to an SMB share configured for guest/anonymous access defeats no technical control -- the share simply had none. Courts have split on whether accessing a resource with no authentication barrier at all counts as 'without authorization' under the CFAA. This is deliberately the 'weakest' legal case among this scenario's findings.
elements: without authorization -- contested here, since no credential or technical barrier was ever in place
cfaa-1030a2-misconfig.penalty: Same range as cfaa-1030a2 if charged, but prosecutorial discretion and case law both trend toward not charging pure unauthenticated access with no barrier defeated -- don't present this step's legal exposure with the same confidence as the SSH/backdoor findings.
cfaa-1030a2-misconfig.evidentiary_note: The Samba connection log shows a guest/nobody-authenticated session reading a specific file -- there's no crafted payload, no bypassed check, just a connection to a share that should never have allowed anonymous access.
